b: Nearly a century into the Academy Awards’ history, firsts are hard to come by, but Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo has notched one this year. The writer-director’s debut feature, Ben’Imana, is Rwanda’s first-ever official submission for best international feature. It’s a fitting first for the country, given that Dusabejambo takes as her subject the conversations around unity and reconciliation that followed its civil war.

Ben’Imana unfolds in 2012, during the twilight of Rwanda’s gacaca courts, which functioned as a form of community-based justice to redress the wrongs committed during the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. While the more common response was silence to protect the country’s fragile peace, over a million Rwandans dared to speak their pain and petition for accountability.

Somewhere in the middle of these two poles stands the film’s protagonist, the steely, principled Vénéranda (Clémentine U. Nyirinkindi). This fiercely protective matriarch is deeply invested in the gacaca courts’ mission of reconciliation. Yet the pregnancy of her daughter, Tina (Kesia Kelly Nishimwe), and the slipping memory of her mother (Arivere Kagoyire) test whether Vénéranda is capable of extending this grace in practice, not just in the abstract.

“I didn’t want it to be digested as a political event,” Dusabejambo says of her hope that the film would strike viewers as something more than a history lesson. “I wanted people to feel it on a personal level: the sisterhood, the motherhood, and all this pain and beauty of family relations.”

I spoke with Dusabejambo this fall in New York as she toured with Ben’Imana ahead of its awards-qualifying release. Our conversation covered what concepts like forgiveness and redemption mean to her now, why mothers became the film’s central narrative focus, and how the value she places on words guided her aesthetic choices.
What does forgiveness mean to you after Ben’Imana?

When I approached the film, I was questioning memory and forgiveness and wondering if it’s possible to heal if we don’t forget. Healing goes with forgiveness, too. Then, as I was doing the research, I was wondering who we have to forgive first. Because most of the time, [resentment] is like drinking poison and then waiting for the other person to die.

I’ve heard that phrase before! I think we have so many clichés to help us because it’s easier in the abstract than it is in real life. There’s one from Fred Rogers, the American children’s TV host, who once said it’s “a decision we make to release a person from the feelings of anger we have at them.”

People have been saying that! It’s really appealing. When you face a situation that makes you feel bad, it’s like you’re hosting a heaviness in your heart. There’s a weight that comes with that offense. Something enters your emotions that wasn’t there before. Every time there’s a reminder, it brings back the same pain. Most of the time, it can even be bigger, because with time, there’s the action that happened, but also what it does to us.
Can forgiveness come from a top-down mandate like the gacaca courts, or must it arise organically from those poised to extend it?

In the aftermath [of the genocide], everything was trying to reinvent itself: the community, the individuals, and then the politics, which are always the politics. In these gacaca courts, it depended on how we decided to look at the past, at what happened, and at what people tried to do with their own wounds, without judgment. When I was approaching this subject, I didn’t want to compare my time to their time, or to compare suffering, because I knew I was walking on a tightrope. All I wanted to do was put on paper and on the screen the weight of living in a post-conflict zone, together with a constant reminder of the past.

How does one individual navigate this? Forgiveness can come from above, from a collectivity, from politics, or from individuals. It comes with time, as people digest what they have lived through. It’s also a matter of choice on so many different levels. Looking back at the past, looking at the present, and thinking of the future all depend on how someone is healing in their own personal process. There’s a collective process, and then there’s a personal process, and they don’t move at the same time or in the same way, because we all deal with things differently.

There’s something I read when I was doing my research: Rwanda chose to go with the gacaca courts because there were so many prisoners, and the country didn’t have the means to take care of all of them. They decided to bring them before these courts, without lawyers, so everyone could see. But then there was another dimension: People needed to know the truth. They needed to know if their loved ones had died, if they could keep waiting for them or not, and the only way to get that information was from the people who were accused of the genocide.

When I was approaching this subject, I saw the gacaca courts as a space for people to speak out, to have conversations, to start something new for the future of the country and for shattered families. We can find murder within the same family, but because of the silence that came after, it was so hard to ask if your sons killed your grandchildren. Those [stories] are in the film. For me, I was just holding up a mirror to what I found, and it was so hard to define any [single] concept of forgiveness or reconciliation. But what I saw in all of this is that people had to make a choice to be able to move forward. There are those who don’t manage, like Suzanne (Isabelle Kabano). Everything’s been said and done, and she can’t find any other reason to continue. Or the grandmother who, at some point, loses her voice. That’s another cultural level: She has no other words to say or describe what happened to her.
How did mothers emerge as the story’s focal point? Is it because they represent both a link to the past and the key to unlocking the future?

The film evolved, and I was being shaped along with it. When I started, I was seeing women on the front line of this reconciliation process, sitting in the gacaca and testifying. But in every genocide, most of the time, it’s men and sons who get killed first and who are involved in the murders. That partly explains why we see women there physically. But then, as I continued to find a way through the story, there was a metaphor of mothers birthing. [Mothers] all have the destiny to give birth. They have to speak the lives of the next generation into [being]. Every generation needs to find a way to talk about what happened, and it [falls to] the people of today to birth a language for transmitting what happened in the past to the next generation.

The mothers were meeting in that room, and no matter how violent and complicated the conversation between them was, I didn’t want them to lose sight of the fact that they were all mothers. Most of the time, when they talk to each other, the terror is what your sons did to our sons. Even if your son was killed, you’re still a mother. This means you saw the innocence of your child, and you dealt with their death at some point: not a physical death, but the death of their innocence. No woman gives birth and says, “Oh, this is a thief that’s coming to the earth.” No, it’s not like that. When they were sitting in that room, it was to look at that identity where they meet, because that’s where they can start rebuilding a foundation for the next generation.

I was already thinking about Rungano Nyoni’s On Becoming a Guinea Fowl before I saw her name in the credits as an associate producer, and I do think Ben’Imana shares with that film a focus on how women are often left to clean up the messes made by violent or abusive men. What were your conversations with her like as the film developed?

Rungano helped us so much. She discovered the film when we were pitching at the Red Sea Film Festival, where she was on the jury. They were all touched by the story. She told me she was moved by these women meeting to think about the future of their generation, putting aside their emotions and suffering as a sacrifice for the foundation of the next generation. This was my first feature film, and we needed so much advice on how to navigate the next chapter of the film. She’s been in the industry for a long time, so I wrote to ask her, and she helped because she liked the idea of the film.

It’s often easy for courtroom dramas or really talky films to develop a flat visual language, but you’re very discerning about when to use more subjective camerawork and lean on close-ups, and even some extreme close-ups. How did you go about developing this aesthetic approach?

I can’t tell you there were any special techniques. Most of the time, I had to go with the emotion that I felt in my heart about every character, every scene, and what it represents. Mostafa El Kashef, who was the director of photography, understood. We took time to sit together, and I told him, “I just want people, when they sit down and watch this film, to feel closer to the characters.” I wanted to film words, which most of the time work in two dimensions: someone who speaks and someone who listens. We all digest the energy of these words at some point, so that’s why doing close-ups and filming the bodies was so important. I didn’t want to use flashbacks, as I knew that these words, finding the proper camera angle, and calculating the lighting were going to help the viewer’s imagination.

I was also experimenting with the positioning of the actors. For example, in one of the gacaca [hearings], you have the mother, the daughter, and the perpetrator. We can’t see the judge, but we can hear him talking. At the end of the day, it helped [the audience] to feel, because the film is also about feeling. It’s 50-50 sound and images, but you can’t give everything to the screen. I needed the viewer to participate in the film.

Names play such an important role in Rwandan culture, from Ben’Imana meaning “children of God” or “the lucky ones” to Suzanne’s daughter Kibeho Abe meaning “so be it.” What’s in a name? Do names shape identity?

Yes, in my language, we say your name explains who you are. Those were concepts [I was exploring] when I started this film. Most of the time, if a proverb exists in Kinyarwanda, it means something, because I come from a culture of oral transmission. When Madeleine says it’s not translated, it’s reserved for those who speak Kinyarwanda. When she says the priest called her Madeleine and her father called her “Uwera Ibiganza,” it’s because “Uwera” means something holy or pure, and “Ibiganza” means hands, so she uses it to clear her name in the court: “My father called me the purest, so my hands are pure.”

Some names are linked, but there are other names I just chose because I needed a name. There’s a version of the script I gave to a friend to read and tell me what he thought about it. He told me, “Did you realize that you have the names of all our neighbors?” We’re made with so many sounds from this community, so every sound that comes out of us is a collective sound of everyone who surrounds us. I took time to readjust and change the names! [laughs]

The film ends with a quote: “In Rwanda, we have chosen to speak of hope to our children, even as we still stand above the bodies of our loved ones, without knowing where they are.” We started by talking about forgiveness, but how do you feel about hope? Is hope itself an act of defiance?

Yes, it requires us to forgive, not forget. Because when you forget, that’s human. We’re humans. But when you forget, it’s so obvious that you can repeat the same thing. That quote, when I read it, meant many things to me, as there were so many sacrifices that people made to be able to coexist in Rwanda. We don’t live in the vocabulary of ethnicity, of Hutus and Tutsis, but people died because of that. People needed justice because of [ethnicity]. The collective decision to remove those ethnic identities—because there’s always someone who benefits from them—is one of the things they chose to put under their feet. They chose to put it down for the sake of the future generation. That’s how I received that quote, and I loved it. It’s a seed they planted in us. It’s up to us to water it so that it can grow.
